[id=doc-053 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-06 | titled Wrenfield onboarding guide for new engineers]
Welcome. This guide is what you read in your first week, and it is deliberately short on process and long on where things are. Your manager will have booked the training your team runs; everything else is here. Wrenfield sells two products. Palisade is the API gateway that sits in front of a customer's own services, and it is the older of the two. Relay moves records between a customer system and our store, and it is the one that grew fastest last year.

The two share nothing but the deployment tooling, and an engineer usually works on one of them. Everything is written down in the channel it belongs to. If you cannot find something, ask in the channel rather than by direct message, so the answer is written down for the next person.

[id=doc-054 | document | by Nils Berg | on 2027-01-12 | titled Glossary of Wrenfield terms]
The words we use, written down because a new joiner asked and nobody could point at anything. Edge node: one of the machines that terminates a customer connection to the Palisade gateway. Edge nodes are stateless and are replaced rather than repaired. Control plane: the part of Palisade that configures the edge nodes. It is not on the request path and an incident on it is usually invisible to customers.

Edge nodes are stateless and are replaced rather than repaired. Control plane: the part of Palisade that configures the edge nodes. It is not on the request path and an incident on it is usually invisible to customers.

title: Glossary of Wrenfield terms

text:
[id=doc-054 | document | by Nils Berg | on 2027-01-12 | titled Glossary of Wrenfield terms]
Dead letter queue: where Relay puts a record that could not be loaded, with the reason attached. Records in it are replayed by hand and the replay tool does not deduplicate. Soak: the period a build sits on staging before it goes to production. A soak is a waiting period, not a test suite, although the acceptance pack runs during it. Error budget: how much unavailability a service is allowed to spend in a period before feature work stops.
body: Dead letter queue: where Relay puts a record that could not be loaded, with the reason attached. Records in it are replayed by hand and the replay tool does not deduplicate. Soak: the period a build sits on staging before it goes to production. A soak is a waiting period, not a test suite, although the acceptance pack runs during it. Error budget: how much unavailability a service is allowed to spend in a period before feature work stops.

title: Glossary of Wrenfield terms

[id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
This section covers how an incident is declared, who is told and what has to be written afterwards. It is the reference the on-call rota points at, and it is reviewed once a quarter by the leadership team. Nothing in it applies to planned maintenance, which has its own page and its own approval path. An incident starts when a customer-visible symptom is confirmed by a second person.
body: This section covers how an incident is declared, who is told and what has to be written afterwards. Nothing in it applies to planned maintenance, which has its own page and its own approval path. An incident starts when a customer-visible symptom is confirmed by a second person.

title: Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling

text:
[id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
The person who confirms it declares the incident in the incidents channel and takes the incident commander role until they hand it over explicitly. The incident commander is not expected to fix anything: the role is to keep the timeline, decide what is communicated and decide when the incident is over. A scribe is appointed for any incident that runs longer than 30 minutes. Communication is on a fixed clock.
body: The person who confirms it declares the incident in the incidents channel and takes the incident commander role until they hand it over explicitly. The incident commander is not expected to fix anything: the role is to keep the timeline, decide what is communicated and decide when the incident is over. A scribe is appointed for any incident that runs longer than 30 minutes. Communication is on a fixed clock.
prefix: [id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
author: Ingrid Halvorsen
title: Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling

text:
[id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
The first customer-facing update goes out within 20 minutes of the incident being declared, and every following update goes out at most every 30 minutes until the incident is closed. Support sends those updates; engineering does not write to customers directly during an incident. After the incident, a written postmortem is due within 5 working days. The postmortem names the trigger, the contributing causes and the actions, and every action has an owner and a date.

The postmortem names the trigger, the contributing causes and the actions, and every action has an owner and a date.

title: Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling

text:
[id=doc-007 | document | by Ingrid Halvorsen | on 2027-01-20 | titled Wrenfield engineering handbook, section 4: incident handling]
Postmortems are blameless and are readable by the whole company. An incident that produced no customer-visible symptom needs no postmortem, only a line in the weekly digest. The escalation ladder for an incident that is not moving is: incident commander, then the engineering manager on the affected team, then the VP of engineering. Do not skip a rung, and do not escalate by direct message.

This is the plain summary of the data processing agreement that every Wrenfield customer contract includes. It is written for engineers, it is not the contract, and where the two disagree the contract wins. Legal keeps the authoritative version. Customer data is processed in the region the customer selects at onboarding. The regions we offer are eu-west, us-east and ap-south.

text:
[id=doc-008 | document | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-02-02 | titled Wrenfield data processing agreement, summary for engineers]
A customer on eu-west has their data stored and processed in eu-west only, and support staff outside the European Union do not get access to it without a written approval from the customer. Sub-processors are listed on the public trust page and customers are told 30 days before a new one is added. A customer may object in writing during those 30 days, and an objection pauses the addition for that customer until it is resolved. Deletion requests are answered within 14 days.

Sub-processors are listed on the public trust page and customers are told 30 days before a new one is added. A customer may object in writing during those 30 days, and an objection pauses the addition for that customer until it is resolved. Deletion requests are answered within 14 days.

text:
[id=doc-008 | document | by Claire Dubois | on 2027-02-02 | titled Wrenfield data processing agreement, summary for engineers]
A deletion request covers the primary store and the search index. Backups are not rewritten: they age out on their own schedule, which is 90 days, and the agreement says so explicitly so nobody promises a customer something we cannot do. Breach notification to the customer is within 72 hours of Wrenfield becoming aware of a breach that affects their data. That clock is not negotiable and it is shorter than the one in the standard terms because two large customers asked for it.

text:
[id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
The Palisade gateway runs on edge nodes in three regions. This runbook covers the edge nodes only: the control plane has its own runbook and the two are deliberately kept apart so an edge problem cannot be fixed by someone who has only read about the control plane. Each region runs at least 4 edge nodes behind a network load balancer. Scaling is manual: there is no autoscaler on the edge tier, on purpose, because a scale event during an incident has bitten us twice.
body: The Palisade gateway runs on edge nodes in three regions. This runbook covers the edge nodes only: the control plane has its own runbook and the two are deliberately kept apart so an edge problem cannot be fixed by someone who has only read about the control plane. Each region runs at least 4 edge nodes behind a network load balancer. Scaling is manual: there is no autoscaler on the edge tier, on purpose, because a scale event during an incident has bitten us twice.

text:
[id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
To add a node, run the provisioning job with the region flag and wait for the health check to pass twice in a row. Draining a node takes the node out of the load balancer, waits for in-flight requests and then stops the process. The drain timeout is 120 seconds. A node that has not drained by then is killed, and the requests it was serving are lost, so drain during a quiet window if you can choose.

text:
[id=doc-009 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-02-08 | titled Palisade gateway runbook, edge nodes]
Certificates are distributed by the platform team and are the same across all edge nodes in a region. A certificate problem is never a single-node problem: if one node is serving a bad certificate, all of them are, and the fix is a redistribution rather than a restart. The log retention on an edge node is 7 days locally, and everything is shipped to the central store where the retention is the customer's own retention window.

[id=doc-043 | document | by Yusuf Demir | on 2027-02-22 | titled Certificate rotation runbook]
This runbook covers the rotation of the Wrenfield edge certificate, which is the certificate a customer sees when they connect to the Palisade gateway. It does not cover the internal mTLS certificates on the admin API: those are rotated by the platform team on their own schedule and nothing here applies to them. A rotation is planned at least a month ahead, because one customer pins the certificate and has 10 working days of notice written into their account.

text:
[id=doc-043 | document | by Yusuf Demir | on 2027-02-22 | titled Certificate rotation runbook]
The notice is sent by the security team, not by support, and it names the exact maintenance window. The maintenance window itself is 01:00 to 02:00 local time in Berlin. That is the quietest hour we have measured across the three regions, and it is written in local time on purpose because the people doing the work are in Berlin. Everything in the scheduler is in UTC and the two differ by an hour in winter and two in summer, which has caught people out.

text:
[id=doc-043 | document | by Yusuf Demir | on 2027-02-22 | titled Certificate rotation runbook]
The rotation is done one region at a time, eu-west first, then us-east, then ap-south, with 15 minutes between regions to watch the error rate. If the error rate moves at all, stop and redistribute the old certificate rather than carrying on. After the rotation, the old certificate stays in the store for 30 days so a rollback is possible, and then it is deleted. Nobody has ever needed the rollback and we keep the 30 days anyway.

[id=doc-010 | document | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-03-01 | titled Relay pipeline architecture notes]
Relay moves records from a customer system into the Wrenfield store and back out again. These notes are the shape of the pipeline as it is built today, written after the Relay Bridge rename so the names are current. Where an older document says Relay Connect it means the same product. The pipeline has four stages: fetch, normalise, validate and load. Fetch talks to the customer system and is the only stage allowed to make outbound network calls.
body: Relay moves records from a customer system into the Wrenfield store and back out again. These notes are the shape of the pipeline as it is built today, written after the Relay Bridge rename so the names are current. Where an older document says Relay Connect it means the same product. The pipeline has four stages: fetch, normalise, validate and load. Fetch talks to the customer system and is the only stage allowed to make outbound network calls.
prefix: [id=doc-010 | document | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-03-01 | titled Relay pipeline architecture notes]
author: Lukas Fenn
title: Relay pipeline architecture notes

text:
[id=doc-010 | document | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-03-01 | titled Relay pipeline architecture notes]
Normalise turns whatever the customer sent into the internal record shape. Validate rejects records that cannot be loaded and writes them to the dead letter queue with the reason attached. Load writes to the store in batches. Back pressure is handled between normalise and validate, and nowhere else. When validate falls behind, normalise blocks, and fetch keeps its own buffer of at most 50000 records before it stops asking the customer system for more.
body: Normalise turns whatever the customer sent into the internal record shape. Validate rejects records that cannot be loaded and writes them to the dead letter queue with the reason attached. Load writes to the store in batches. Back pressure is handled between normalise and validate, and nowhere else. When validate falls behind, normalise blocks, and fetch keeps its own buffer of at most 50000 records before it stops asking the customer system for more.
prefix: [id=doc-010 | document | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-03-01 | titled Relay pipeline architecture notes]
author: Lukas Fenn
title: Relay pipeline architecture notes

text:
[id=doc-010 | document | by Lukas Fenn | on 2027-03-01 | titled Relay pipeline architecture notes]
That buffer is the only place where records live outside a stage. The pipeline is single-tenant: every customer gets their own pipeline instance, and one customer's back pressure cannot slow another customer down. That costs us money and we have decided it is worth it. Failures in fetch are retried with an exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds. Failures in load are not retried inside the pipeline at all: they go to the dead letter queue and are replayed by hand.

Failures in load are not retried inside the pipeline at all: they go to the dead letter queue and are replayed by hand.

[id=doc-045 | document | by Sofia Marchetti | on 2027-03-10 | titled Palisade release process]
This is how a Palisade release is cut, from the freeze on the branch to the note that goes out to customers. It is the process for a scheduled release. A hotfix follows the incident process instead and skips most of this. The branch is cut on the Monday of the release week. From that moment only fixes go on it, and every fix needs a named reviewer from a different team than the author.
body: This is how a Palisade release is cut, from the freeze on the branch to the note that goes out to customers. It is the process for a scheduled release. A hotfix follows the incident process instead and skips most of this. The branch is cut on the Monday of the release week. From that moment only fixes go on it, and every fix needs a named reviewer from a different team than the author.
prefix: [id=doc-045 | document | by Sofia Marchetti | on 2027-03-10 | titled Palisade release process]
author: Sofia Marchetti
title: Palisade release process

text:
[id=doc-045 | document | by Sofia Marchetti | on 2027-03-10 | titled Palisade release process]
The build that goes to staging is the build that goes to production: we do not rebuild between the two, so an artefact that fails on staging is thrown away rather than patched. Staging soak is 48 hours. During the soak, the quality team runs the acceptance pack twice, once at the start and once at the end, and both runs have to be clean. A soak that is cut short needs the engineering manager to say so in writing.
body: The build that goes to staging is the build that goes to production: we do not rebuild between the two, so an artefact that fails on staging is thrown away rather than patched. Staging soak is 48 hours. During the soak, the quality team runs the acceptance pack twice, once at the start and once at the end, and both runs have to be clean. A soak that is cut short needs the engineering manager to say so in writing.
prefix: [id=doc-045 | document | by Sofia Marchetti | on 2027-03-10 | titled Palisade release process]
author: Sofia Marchetti
title: Palisade release process

text:
[id=doc-045 | document | by Sofia Marchetti | on 2027-03-10 | titled Palisade release process]
The release note is written by the product manager and reviewed by support before it goes out, because support are the ones who will be asked about it. It goes out on the morning of the release, not the night before. General availability is a separate decision from the release itself. A release can ship to production and stay behind a flag for weeks, and the general availability date is the one that goes on the launch page.
body: The release note is written by the product manager and reviewed by support before it goes out, because support are the ones who will be asked about it. It goes out on the morning of the release, not the night before. General availability is a separate decision from the release itself. A release can ship to production and stay behind a flag for weeks, and the general availability date is the one that goes on the launch page.

[id=doc-046 | document | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-03-15 | titled Relay operations guide, running a backfill]
A backfill replays historical records through the Relay pipeline for one customer. It is the most dangerous routine thing we do, because it writes to the same store as the live pipeline, and this guide exists so it is done the same way every time. Before anything, the customer is told. A backfill changes what they see in their own reports and they have asked us more than once not to surprise them. The notice goes out from the account owner, at least 3 working days before the backfill starts.
body: A backfill replays historical records through the Relay pipeline for one customer. It is the most dangerous routine thing we do, because it writes to the same store as the live pipeline, and this guide exists so it is done the same way every time. Before anything, the customer is told. A backfill changes what they see in their own reports and they have asked us more than once not to surprise them. The notice goes out from the account owner, at least 3 working days before the backfill starts.
prefix: [id=doc-046 | document | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-03-15 | titled Relay operations guide, running a backfill]
author: Elena Sokolova
title: Relay operations guide, running a backfill

text:
[id=doc-046 | document | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-03-15 | titled Relay operations guide, running a backfill]
The backfill runs at a reduced rate so the live pipeline is not starved. The reduced rate is 200 records a second, which is a quarter of what the pipeline does at full speed. A backfill at full speed has caused two of the stalls we have had this year. A backfill is never run during the nightly reconciliation window. The reconciliation job and a backfill writing to the same store at the same time produce duplicates that nobody can untangle afterwards, and the replay tool does not deduplicate.
body: The backfill runs at a reduced rate so the live pipeline is not starved. The reduced rate is 200 records a second, which is a quarter of what the pipeline does at full speed. A backfill at full speed has caused two of the stalls we have had this year. A backfill is never run during the nightly reconciliation window. The reconciliation job and a backfill writing to the same store at the same time produce duplicates that nobody can untangle afterwards, and the replay tool does not deduplicate.
prefix: [id=doc-046 | document | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-03-15 | titled Relay operations guide, running a backfill]
author: Elena Sokolova
title: Relay operations guide, running a backfill

text:
[id=doc-046 | document | by Elena Sokolova | on 2027-03-15 | titled Relay operations guide, running a backfill]
When the backfill finishes, the record counts are compared with the customer's own counts before the pipeline is put back to full speed. A mismatch is an incident, not a retry.
body: When the backfill finishes, the record counts are compared with the customer's own counts before the pipeline is put back to full speed. A mismatch is an incident, not a retry.

text:
[id=doc-055 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-04-19 | titled Postmortem INC-2027-014, edge outage on 11 April]
Summary. On 11 April the eu-west edge tier stopped serving traffic for 41 minutes, and us-east followed 12 minutes later. Customers saw connection failures rather than errors, because the failure was below the application layer. Trigger. A certificate distribution job pushed a certificate with the wrong chain to every edge node in eu-west. The job is not new and has run every month for a year.
body: Summary. On 11 April the eu-west edge tier stopped serving traffic for 41 minutes, and us-east followed 12 minutes later. Customers saw connection failures rather than errors, because the failure was below the application layer. Trigger. A certificate distribution job pushed a certificate with the wrong chain to every edge node in eu-west. The job is not new and has run every month for a year.
prefix: [id=doc-055 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-04-19 | titled Postmortem INC-2027-014, edge outage on 11 April]
author: Diego Alvarez
title: Postmortem INC-2027-014, edge outage on 11 April

text:
[id=doc-055 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-04-19 | titled Postmortem INC-2027-014, edge outage on 11 April]
What was new was a change to the chain builder three days earlier, which nobody connected to the certificate job. Detection. The first alert fired 90 seconds after the distribution, which is the fastest detection we have had. The incident was declared 4 minutes later, after a second person confirmed the symptom. Resolution. The old certificate was redistributed.
body: What was new was a change to the chain builder three days earlier, which nobody connected to the certificate job. Detection. The first alert fired 90 seconds after the distribution, which is the fastest detection we have had. The incident was declared 4 minutes later, after a second person confirmed the symptom. Resolution. The old certificate was redistributed.
prefix: [id=doc-055 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-04-19 | titled Postmortem INC-2027-014, edge outage on 11 April]
author: Diego Alvarez
title: Postmortem INC-2027-014, edge outage on 11 April

text:
[id=doc-055 | document | by Diego Alvarez | on 2027-04-19 | titled Postmortem INC-2027-014, edge outage on 11 April]
The redistribution itself took 6 minutes; the rest of the 41 minutes was spent deciding that redistribution was the right move, which is the part worth fixing. Actions. Diego Alvarez to add a certificate chain check to the distribution job by 2027-05-15. Nils Berg to write down what makes a redistribution the right call, so the next person does not have to work it out during an incident. Both actions are tracked in the platform team backlog. This postmortem is blameless.

This is the shape of the Palisade plan for the rest of the year, written after the June planning session. It is a plan and it will move, which is why it is a note and not a commitment. The theme for the second half is the admin API. It is the oldest part of the product, it is the part customers integrate with most deeply, and it is the part with the least written down about it. The work is a rewrite of the authentication path first and the rest afterwards.

[id=doc-057 | document | by Sofia Marchetti | on 2027-06-21 | titled Palisade product notes for the second half of the year]

It has no general availability date and will not get one before the summer freeze is over, because putting a date on it now would only be a date we later move. The edge tier gets no feature work this half. It is stable, it is well understood, and every hour spent on it is an hour not spent on the admin API. The exception is anything an incident forces on us. We are not adding a region this year.
